title: Environmental Bacteriophages as Biocontrol Agents Against Waterborne Multidrug-Resistant Pathogens Across South Asia
content: Waterborne multidrug-resistant pathogens pose a significant public health concern in South Asia, yet the studies regarding environmental phages remain underrepresented in existing reviews. This narrative review examines phage ecology and evaluates phages targeting five waterborne pathogens: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Salmonella Typhi, and Vibrio cholerae. It focuses on Nepal, India, and Bangladesh, while comparing available findings with research from Iran, Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and South America. Studies reveal that South Asian rivers have diverse phage communities and phage activity against all five pathogens. Metagenomic analysis performed in the Yamuna River of India documented 28,993 viral contigs, out of which 19% were linked to the pathogenic bacterial hosts, while crAssphage was detected in 72% of the samples from Bagmati River, Nepal. Phage administration reduced Klebsiella loads in mice by 3-7log10 CFU/mL in Nepal and vibriophage abundance was reported to predict cholera burden one week in advance. No field deployment for water treatment has been reported in South Asia. Compared with Iran, where phage cocktails reduced bacterial loads in hospital wastewater, South Asian research remains largely at the isolation and characterization stage. Priorities include systematic pathogen monitoring, standardized genomic methods, phage cocktail development, and regionally appropriate regulation.
